data.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirement enforcement
data.description:
The Trump administration is delaying the implementation of controversial Medicaid work requirements, giving states an extra six months to prepare. 

The work requirements, which Republicans established in the One Big Beautiful Bill last year, will still technically go into effect Jan. 1. But states will have an optional “hold harmless” transition period that will run through the end of June, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) said Friday. 

States that implement the hold harmless period will assess whether individuals meet the work requirement or are excluded from it, but they will not deny applications or disenroll otherwise eligible individuals solely for failure to meet the requirement, CMS said. 

The delay will also give states an opportunity to learn from the early months of implementation to “identify and address workforce training needs and improve the beneficiary experience,” CMS said. 

Once the requirements are enforced, millions of Americans will have to start proving they work, volunteer or attend school at least 80 hours per month — or risk getting kicked off their health insurance. 

“States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries—at scale and for the long term,” Deputy Administrator and Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Dan Brillman said in a statement.

“If the state can use data to show that someone is working or qualifies for an exclusion, that person should not have to track down paperwork to prove it,” he added. “And when someone needs support, they should know exactly what to do, when to do it, and where to go.” 

CMS has been facing pressure from states and Democratic lawmakers to delay the effective date.

States said the implementation was rushed from the start, as the law gave less than 18 months from enactment to go-live date. They said they weren’t given enough time to set up the verification systems needed to enforce the new requirements. 

Advocates said the rushed implementation risked millions more people becoming entangled in paperwork and administrative red tape, and losing coverage. 

According to the Congressional Budget Office, about 5 million fewer people are expected to be enrolled in Medicaid over the next 10 years because of the work requirements; most of those people are expected to be uninsured. 

Last month, a federal judge put more uncertainty into the process when he ruled CMS was too strict when it outlined how people can be considered too “medically frail” to work.  

Democratic-led states had sued CMS over its regulation, charging it went further than what Congress intended.

data.title: House Democrat calls FAA stop 'quite disturbing'
data.description:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) called the nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday “quite disturbing.”

“This is quite disturbing and pretty extraordinary of a action taken,” Garcia said during an appearance on MS NOW. “Whatever it is, I think deserves as much transparency as possible.”

“The impact is going to be immense,” the congressman added.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in a post on social platform X that the ground stop was issued “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” he added.

The agency shared an advisory citing “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety” for the ground stop, according to The New York Times. The advisory is not currently listed on the FAA’s website.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage – out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” the FAA wrote on social media.

“Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”

Garcia said if it is a “technical issue … then I think we just need to know what that is immediately.”

“The amount of people that are going to be grounded across this country is going to cause major interruptions and chaos,” he added.

data.title: Jeffries outlines Democratic plans for Medicare expansion
data.description:
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Friday endorsed efforts to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand the program, as Democrats try to navigate internal tensions around a progressive push for Medicare for All. 

During a conference in Denver about the future of the Democratic party, Jeffries outlined the healthcare legislative priorities Democrats plan to tackle once he takes over as House speaker in January. 

Jeffries said the party must first undo Republican cuts to Medicaid funding and restore the Affordable Care Act’s temporary enhanced premium tax credits that Democrats provided during the COVID-19 pandemic. 

While he stopped short of endorsing Medicare for All, Jeffries said Democrats need to go further than merely restoring what Republicans took. 

“I think we’ve got to lower the age of eligibility as it relates to Medicare. I think we’ve got to make sure that we cover hearing, vision, and dental, and we’ve got to make sure that every child in America can be able to see a doctor with high-quality affordable health care,” Jeffries said. 

“These are steps that we can take.” 

Medicare for All has become a critical issue on the left over the last decade, largely due to the efforts of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.)  

Buoyed by the victories of candidates like Abdul El-Sayed (D) in Michigan, progressives in the House and Senate are expected to make a significant push for single-payer healthcare.   

After the election, Sanders called on Democrats to lower the Medicare age to 55 through budget reconciliation, which can pass on a party-line vote, as an “immediate first step” towards Medicare for All. 

Sanders also said Democrats should add dental, vision and hearing coverage to Medicare and expand children’s coverage. 

In Denver Jeffries, who has been criticized by progressive activists for not being bold enough and for being friendly to special interests, was repeatedly heckled by protesters. 

“Medicare for all now!” yelled one.  

“Why should we trust you?” one shouted, while another called Jeffries a “traitor.”  

But unlike his Senate counterpart Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Jeffries faces no serious competition in his bid to be elected House Speaker.  

“Remember y’all, I grew up in Brooklyn,” he said with a smile.

data.title: Fed unveils 2027 calendar, confirming October meeting will not include rates vote
data.description:
The Federal Reserve on Thursday released next year’s schedule for its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), confirming that one meeting will feature discussions on strategy and not a vote on interest rates.

The Fed said in a release the FOMC will meet eight times in 2027, with the first meeting in late January and subsequent meetings at six-week intervals.

On the second and final day of those meetings, the panel will vote on the federal funds rate, with the exception of its gathering on Oct. 26-27 of next year.

That meeting, the Fed said, will be “dedicated to the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues.”

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced the change last month, after FOMC officials held interest rates steady at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent. The central bank chair said the committee is making the switch for “straightforward” reasons.

“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals,” he told reporters. 

“But it’s equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations — for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point,” Warsh added.

Warsh raised a change to the FOMC’s schedule during the panel’s July meeting, according to the minutes.

The first-year chair “observed that six scheduled meetings” each year, held every two months, would “allow more information to accumulate between meetings” than under the status quo, the minutes noted.

Warsh said last month he expects for the FOMC to have two meetings dedicated to strategy discussions and six for setting monetary policy in 2028. Under the Federal Reserve Act, the panel must meet at least four times per year.

Jason Furman, the chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under former President Obama, praised Warsh’s tweak to the Fed calendar as a “great move” last month.

“I have long thought the Fed spends too much time on the immediate and not nearly enough time thinking about longer-term strategy,” Furman wrote on social platform X. 

The change marks the latest example of Warsh, who succeeded former Fed Chair Jerome Powell in May, putting his imprint on the central bank.

The FOMC’s policy statements have skewed away from including “forward guidance,” information about the likely future conduct of monetary policy.

Warsh has also been alone among 19 committee officials in not providing a “dot” prediction about future rates decisions for either of the FOMC’s two quarterly economic projections since he took over.

The Fed chair has laid out his preference for limiting future projections throughout his nearly six months in charge, saying in July market participants “are learning to play the ball, not the referee” without them.

“I understand the desire for rolling forecasts and commentary from this committee. But for our part, we need to observe market reaction to developments, direct and unfiltered,” Warsh told reporters at the time.

data.title: Mullin: No indication of 'nefarious attack' on FAA as DHS investigates root cause of telecom outage
data.description:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stressed that Americans flying Friday are safe, even as he said the Department of Homeland Security would continue to seek the root cause of a telecom outage that pushed the government to ground flights.

“This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA,” Mullin said while fielding questions outside the White House, referencing the Federal Aviation Administration.

“There was no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunication outage as of right now.”

 But pressed by reporters, Mullin said the agency would not rule out a cyber attack.

“Of course, through DHS, we’re getting a ton of calls saying, ‘Is this a terrorist attack? Is this a terrorist attack?’ Everybody’s safe. There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they’re flying or anything like that. I just want to make sure everybody’s at ease about that. As we investigate what caused this, you always got to assume that as many cyber attacks that take place that you make that assumption. So, but as of right now, that’s not known,” he told reporters.

“We’re going to continue to work. The first thing we want to do is make sure we restore the communications, we get all the flights on the ground, and then we get back normal operations. But we’re going to continue to work to find out what the root of the cause is.”

data.title: Angie Nixon fires back at Carville: 'He needs to go retire'
data.description:
Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon (D), who lost to GOP incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody in last week’s midterm elections, called Democratic strategist James Carville a “racist” in a Thursday night interview, adding he should “go retire.”

“That man is a racist,” Nixon told former MS NOW commentator Joy-Ann Reid during an appearance on The Joy Reid Show.

“The way in which he talks and how he has continued to downplay the work that I was able to do and the work that other folks have been able to do, other Black candidates, is just really mad disrespectful,” she added. “He needs to go retire and stop being disrespectful.”

Nixon’s remarks came after Carville, during a conversation with Gen Z for Change founder Aidan Kohn-Murphy on the Democratic strategist’s “Politics War Room” podcast, called Nixon “a uniquely uninspiring Senate candidate.”

“You may like her politics. She was not a good statewide candidate. She was not a good fit for the state of Florida,” Carville said.

The Florida Democrat directly addressed Carville’s post-midterm commentary, saying, “You were very disrespectful. And, you know, it doesn’t matter if you don’t like me, I didn’t drag anyone down.” 

“James Carville, your analysis is whack. It is not truthful and it is rooted in the white supremacy that continued to run this country,” Nixon added. 

Florida is one of the few historically-red states in which Republicans maintained their stronghold post-Election Day, as Democrats secured sweeping victories across the country — claiming both congressional chambers and flipping GOP-held seats in battleground states like Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Kansas, among others.

Nixon lost the Senate race to her GOP opponent by a little less than three points, according to Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s election results partner. The state’s gubernatorial race also swung in the Republicans’ favor, with Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) defeating Democrat David Jolly by a little over one point.

Earlier, Nixon called the contest a “missed opportunity” for Democrats.

“If want to continue to profess that we care about Black people and Hispanic communities, then we need to invest in them,” Nixon said on “The Don Lemon Show” earlier this week. “Black women, especially Black people, are seen as the backbone of the party, and so they need to not only invest … in our labor so to speak, they need to really invest in our leadership.”

Updated at 5:20 p.m. EST

data.title: Fate of Trump's D.C. golf course makeover at East Potomac Park hangs before federal judge
data.description:
A federal judge is set to rule this weekend on whether the Trump administration can move forward with its planned closure of East Potomac Park and the historic public golf course there, with the judge signaling during a lengthy hearing on Friday that she was not poised to allow it, at least for now.  

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes pushed back on claims from Justice Department (DOJ) lawyers that the closure, which President Trump has said will happen on Sunday is meant to address urgent public safety risks and is separate from a broader proposed development project the president has been angling for.

“Why all of the sudden on Nov. 15 do these justify closing down the entire park?” Reyes asked Adam Gustafson, the principal deputy assistant attorney general for DOJ’s Energy and Natural Resources Division.

The judge, who sits on the federal bench in D.C., is expected to rule by the end of Saturday.

Friday’s was the latest in a series of contentious, hourslong hearings over the project in recent months, in which the Biden-appointed judge has frequently scolded DOJ officials for seemingly misrepresenting the plans as different from the president’s public comments.  

“I’m trying to figure out which iteration of me not paying attention to the president I’m supposed to go with today,” Reyes said on Friday.  

The judge previously said she intended to tap former U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jessie Lui to investigate whether Trump administration lawyers may have “committed ethical violations” during the ongoing litigation. 

“That does not mean in any way, shape or form that I think anything untoward has happened,” Reyes said. “It only means that I think there is enough smoke that someone needs to consider whether there’s been fire.”  

In turn, the Justice Department has accused Reyes of overstepping her authority and demanded she recuse from the case. She has refused to do so.  

The judge has already barred the Trump administration from cutting any more trees at East Potomac Park unless they pose an imminent risk to public safety. Even then, Reyes said the administration must provide 24-hour notice.  

The Trump administration has appealed that ruling to the D.C. Circuit. 

The future of East Potomac Park has been uncertain for months, following the National Park Service’s termination of its lease with the National Links Trust, the local nonprofit that had operated the courses there since the coronavirus pandemic.  

Months after Trump posted on Truth Social a proposed design for a new course, the department abruptly removed hundreds of trees from the park as confused golfers played just feet away.

A preservationist group and local golfers who are suing to stop the redevelopment also want Reyes to block the park from closing on Sunday, when the National Links Trust (NLT) has said it would cede operational control of the courses there.

“It’s not, as you were saying earlier, just a massive coincidence that NLT suddenly up and decided to leave as of the very same day that the president directed defendants to close the park,” argued Catherine Carroll, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs. 

The Trump administration terminated a lease with NLT last year, and the president has said the property would close this month so construction on an 18-hole championship length facility can begin.

The new proposed course, which would be designed by famed architect Tom Fazio, calls for a championship-level facility that would stretch more than 8,000 yards from the back tees, making it one of the largest in the country.  

Critics from around the golf world have argued such a design will reduce accessibility for amateur golfers who have long been able to play at East Potomac, which today primarily caters to beginners and more casual golfers, at an affordable price. 

The judge polled the courtroom early into the hearing, asking attendees to raise their hands if they had “strong views” about the redesign. The “vast majority” did, she noted.  

Gustafson said the Fazio concept is not final, and the Interior Department could still “change its mind” pending public feedback. 

Major questions about the project’s feasibility and cost remain.  

A damaged seawall, which has been in poor condition since the Obama administration, leads to frequent flooding at the park and will cost hundreds of millions of dollars to repair. 

The government has so far provided few details on where financing for the seawall repair would come from, while attorneys for the administration pointed to its condition in arguing the peninsula needs to be closed off to the public.  

Reyes drilled down on the government’s assertions on Friday, questioning what changed that required an immediate closure when deteriorating conditions have been documented for more than a decade. 

“Just days after 30,000-plus people ran around Ohio Drive, it is an emergent situation,” she said, referring to the Marine Corps marathon last month that went directly around Hains Point. “So, tell me what happened.” 

Gustafson deflected when faced with similar lines of questioning throughout the hearing, pointing several times only to safety and the lack of an operator as justification for the imminent closure.

Reyes called the latter a “self-inflicted” issue, comparing it to a situation in which a person starts a fire at their home and then tries to recoup insurance money.  

” You’re the one who set the house on fire,” she told DOJ.

data.title: Live updates: FAA issues nationwide ground stop; Supreme Court to hear asylum ban case
data.description:
Editor’s Note: Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) earlier this week said they would not back Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for another term as Democratic leader. Slotkin has said she is seeking change, and that a new leader would need to show a plan for the first 100 days. An earlier version of this story included incorrect information.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. flights; a measure used only in extreme circumstances.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the move on Friday, citing a “communication issue.” The ground stop prevents all flights from taking off from U.S. airports, but flights currently in the air will be allowed to land.

The Supreme Court on Friday said it would take up a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s asylum restrictions. The court will rule by July on whether the ban is legal.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) announced Thursday night that he would challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to become the next majority leader of the upper chamber in the next Congress. Democratic senators have begun taking sides in the leadership fight.

“I think that we heard loud and clear from the American people that they want to end the war in Iran and bring down prices,” Van Hollen told MS NOW’s Jen Psaki. “We should do it now. We shouldn’t say we’re going to wait till January.”

Follow live below.

data.title: Hassett denies report he is leaving White House
data.description:
Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council (NEC), pushed back Friday on a report that he will depart the Trump administration in the coming weeks.

He told CNBC’s Eamon Javers through text that the report is “not true.”

The White House also denied the report, writing on X, “There is no factual basis for this reporting. Kevin Hassett is a key member of President Trump’s economic team and will continue working to advance President Trump’s economic policies.” 

Semafor reported earlier Friday that Hassett “has been inquiring about roles outside the administration,” and that it had nothing to do with the GOP’s losses in the midterm elections. 

Hassett, who chaired the Council of Economic Advisers during Trump’s first term, has helmed the NEC for the entirety of the president’s second term so far.

Former President Clinton established the council in 1993, and its members advise the president on domestic and international economic policy issues.

The NEC director has vocally defended the president and his economic policies, including his tariffs and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, on CNBC, Fox Business and other cable channels. Days before the midterm elections, Hassett touted the economy and downplayed Americans’ concerns about the cost of living.

“All the things that have made the economy great, means that affordability crisis, it’s a myth,” Hassett said on Fox Business’s “Kudlow.”

Hassett also echoed Trump in criticizing former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell for not backing further interest rate cuts the last two years. Hassett was one of multiple candidates to succeed Powell, with the president ultimately selecting Kevin Warsh.

Multiple administration officials have already left the White House since the midterms, which saw Democrats capture control of both chambers of Congress.

Stephen Miller replaced Susie Wiles as Trump’s chief of staff this week, and Richard Walters has also left his role as deputy chief of staff.

Four Justice Department officials have also departed since the midterms, including Harmeet Dhillon, who led the department’s Civil Rights Division.

data.title: FAA orders nationwide ground stop
data.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. flights, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed on Friday.

“The [FAA] issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” Duffy wrote on the social platform X. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

The ground stop prevents all flights from taking off from U.S. airports, but flights currently in the air will be allowed to land.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
